extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics; graduate students and scholars of history of science; readers interested in 19th-century mathematical culture
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply evaluative dimensions used in chapters on 19th- and 20th-century mathematics (topics include everyday numeracy, professionalization, rigor, pedagogy, statistics, technology, and globalization). Useful for assessing historical research questions, themes, and standards emphasized in the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of arithmetic education
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent was education in arithmetic available at this time, and to whom?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter poses this as a primary research question for everyday numeracy: consider geographic and social variation (e.g., Victorian Britain vs elsewhere), availability across classes and genders, and the limitation that satisfactory global answers are impossible without extensive local sources; hence use illustrative case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of arithmetic education and skills imparted by textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: What form did this education take, and what skills were imparted by contemporary textbooks?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine curricula, emphasis on memory/rote or applied problem-solving, and what textbook exercises aimed to teach (reckoning, household management, commerce, demography, social reform). Use textbook content as evidence for skills taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems of weights, measures, and currency and facilitation efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: What systems of weights, measures and currency were in place, and what efforts were made to facilitate their use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate standardization (e.g., metric system), state interventions, institutional prescriptions, and transitional arrangements that made everyday computation easier or harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other resources for everyday numerical computations
rubrics_metrics.description: What other resources were available to facilitate everyday numerical computations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include aids such as tables, tools, models, instruments, and institutional supports (e.g., statistical offices, pamphlets). Assess accessibility and practical utility for non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure to data and numerical information in everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent were people exposed to data and numerical information in everyday life?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider circulation of statistics, newspapers, public reports, and how increasing data-collection and publication affected lay experience and expectations of numeracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional foundations of professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalization developed through institutions that promoted research and trained a new generation of researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence and role of research institutions, specialized schools, professorships, and how institutional structures enabled a class of professional mathematicians paid to do and disseminate research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation in admissions and teaching as hallmark of modern schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation in admissions and in teaching methods were hallmarks (e.g., of the École Polytechnique) for forming new mathematical elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use admissions policies and pedagogical innovations as indicators of a shift toward training technical elites (engineers) rather than traditional humanist education; compare across national models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social status and linkage to meritocracy/state
rubrics_metrics.description: The social status of higher mathematics and its linkage to meritocratic/state structures (e.g., gateway to higher echelons under Napoleon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how mathematics served as social mobility gateway, its symbolic role in forming technocratic elites, and ties between mathematicians and state institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing national educational models (French vs Prussian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different national models (French École Polytechnique vs Prussian Bildung) represent alternative aims: technical training vs spiritual/neo-humanist development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare curricular emphases (engineering/mathematics as professional training versus classical education stressing Greek/Latin and 'Bildung') and their long-term influence on professional mathematics and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization indicated by proliferation of journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing specialization manifested by many journals devoted exclusively to pure and applied mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the proliferation of specialized periodicals as a metric of professionalization and disciplinary specialization; examine editorial policies and scope to judge degree of specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of rigor ('better proofs')
rubrics_metrics.description: A new, more abstract and autonomous sense of rigour changed what could be said and what had to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work by whether it meets newer rigorous standards (abstractness, autonomy from naive intuition), and whether rigor functions as a tool for discovery and legitimization rather than mere formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorization of analysis/calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical analysis became rigorized (Cauchy → stable form by Weierstrass, Dedekind, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use acceptance of precise definitions (limits, epsilons, set-theoretic foundations) and stable formulations as criteria for judging the maturity and acceptability of analytical results in the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of genuinely new subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: New subjects are those not simple extensions of earlier work (e.g., Galois' foundations, Gauss' redefinition of number theory, non-Euclidean geometries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge novelty by conceptual discontinuity from past work: emergence of new theories, axiomatic approaches, and fields that required new foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different kinds of mathematical answers (existence vs constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift toward answers that are more conceptual and sometimes non-constructive (e.g., proving existence without exhibiting solutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether results provide explicit constructions or only existence/qualitative information; recognize that conceptual/non-constructive answers became valued as valid mathematical contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify 'worldviews' as analytical category
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'worldviews' — actors' category vs observers' category — and distinguish related terms (Weltansicht vs Weltanschauung).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For studies invoking 'worldviews', require explicit definition and methodological stance (are you analyzing actors' self-understandings or imposing an observer's typology?), and heed historical semantic shifts (e.g., Humboldt's Weltansichten).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and intellectual contexts for studying worldviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider specific institutional/intellectual contexts (École Polytechnique, Cambridge Analytical Society, Berlin methodological commitments, tentative unified worldviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing mathematical worldviews, situate arguments in concrete institutional settings and trace methodological/philosophical commitments of mathematicians in those settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of standardized measurement systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of standards (e.g., metric system: meter, gram, liter) is a key criterion in evaluating scientific/technical modernization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track state-driven standardization efforts and their adoption as an index of technical modernization and the facilitation of numerical computation and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth of statistical data-collection and state use
rubrics_metrics.description: Gathering of statistical data (census, birth/death/crime/education/economic data) and formation of statistical bodies indicate the rise of 'experts in calculation' and state capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the scale, institutionalization, and uses of statistical collection (policy, conscription, social control) and the emergence of statistical expertise (Malthus, Babbage, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of probabilistic/statistical reasoning across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability/statistics entered new domains (economics, heredity, kinetic theory, blackbody radiation) and became central to modeling and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the penetration of probabilistic methods into disciplines and technologies; measure significance by methodological adoption (Maxwell, Boltzmann, Galton, Planck) and impact on conceptual frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics' role in technological change (transport, electromagnetism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics underpinned technological change—transportation and electromagnetism were central threads—and improved instruments enabled more accurate data and theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical cases by tracing mathematical contributions to design, modeling, instrumentation, and how mathematical precision enabled technological innovation and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation in mathematics (material practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation = 'to show' or 'to demonstrate' a mathematical concept; closely linked to educational practices (drawing, modeling, demonstrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use and effectiveness of representational media (drawings, models, haptic tools) in teaching and dissemination; consider their epistemic and pedagogical roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical intuition/Anschauung and two-step pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical intuition (Anschauung) involves visualization and haptic sense; pedagogical two-step: direct experience with objects (cubes, spheres), then abstraction to geometrical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of concrete teaching aids and staged pedagogy (concrete → abstract) as criteria for evaluating instructional approaches and their claimed effectiveness (advocated by Fröbel, Pestalozzi, Klein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material models as pedagogical and symbolic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Models served both as visual/material embodiments of concepts and as status symbols conveying a mathematician's scientific approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both instrumental pedagogical value and symbolic/signalling function of models in institutional and intellectual contexts (e.g., Klein's collections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeracy in the Information Age: data and probabilistic literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeracy expanded from arithmetic to include statistical averages, data trends, and probabilistic predictions; essential for functioning in modern life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing modern numeracy, include statistical/data literacy and understanding of algorithmic/uncertainty issues; recognize that many users need conceptual competence rather than technical mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of educational access and measuring numeracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of schooling made numeracy a broadly expected competence; invention of the term 'numeracy' (1959) and organizations (International Bureau of Education, UNESCO) enabled global data collection on mathematical attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indicators such as schooling coverage, gender parity, international assessments, and institutional data-collection practices to measure numeracy expansion and disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics, wars, and globalization shaping the mathematical profession
rubrics_metrics.description: International relations, two world wars, Cold War competition, migration, and institutional shifts (e.g., US dominance after WWII) shaped mathematical communities and research trajectories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze professional development in historical periods (pre-1945, post-1945 Cold War, post-1990) by tracing migration, institutional expansion, funding/policy contexts, and geopolitical pressures impacting research agendas.
